text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--At the end of 1996 Danes owed 35.7 billion crowns in tax. Half of the debt was a consequence of the activities of asset-strippers, Tax Minister Carsten Koch says.
--Rising employment means that there is now room in the job market for the socially marginalised, such as those with histories of drug or alcohol abuse.

--Danish state railways' freight division is negotiating with counterparts in the Benelux countries, Austria and Switzerland with a view to collaborating in competition with the heavyweight German and French rail companies and road hauliers.
--Banks are prepared to compensate clients who suffer financially as a result of bank error in property transactions.
--Business school professor Niels Lunde warns of a repeat of the property collapse of the 1980s if the government continues to erode the value of mortgage tax relief.
--Carlsberg dominates the Danish market to such an extent that the EU is considering examining its position, but group director Flemming Lindeloev does not expect EU restrictions.

--Over 12 months A.P.Moeller's shares have increased in value by 37 billion crowns, a Price Waterhouse study for Borsen shows. Sophus Berendsen, Novo Nordisk, Tele Danmark and Carlsberg have also given good returns to their shareholders, while Lauritzen Holding shares have declined.
--Cut-price airline DebonAir has had such success with its flights out of Copenhagen that it is now opening new routes between Copenhagen and Stockholm and Stockholm and London.

--This year's crop of new graduates have an easier time finding work than their predecessors five years ago, due to the strengthening economy and employers' increased willingness to employ new staff, says a Copenhagen University official.
--In contrast to the United States and many European countries Denmark has maintained a minimal gap between rich and poor in its society during a time of strong economic growth, a new analysis shows.
